Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (SJIA) can mimic leukemia with spiking fevers, evanescent rash (not reported but often absent early), arthralgia/myalgia, and even transient cytopenias—but severe nocturnal leg pain is atypical, and bruising is not a feature unless macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) develops, which would usually be accompanied by rapidly worsening lab abnormalities (e.g., ferritin >10,000 ng/mL, coagulopathy). Aplastic anemia explains fatigue and bruising (pancytopenia) and may cause low-grade fever due to immune dysregulation or infection, but bone pain is rare unless severe marrow collapse triggers compensatory extramedullary hematopoiesis (uncommon in young children). Neuroblastoma—especially stage 4—can present with bone pain (often lower extremities), fever, pallor, and bruising (from marrow metastases or DIC); however, it typically has more subacute weight loss, periorbital ecchymoses ('raccoon eyes'), or abdominal mass—none reported here. Less likely considerations include infectious osteomyelitis (usually focal, not bilateral/nocturnal-dominant), mononucleosis (fatigue/fever but no bruising/bone pain), or ITP (bruising/fatigue but no fever/bone pain).
